status: agent review, 2026-10-26, under the researcher's R6 approval of the process; agent judgements, for the researcher to read
method: First pass: one blind model reviewer read all 144 bank v2 questions against the full lists of bank v1 (576) and the historical banks (1,472 distinct) and classified each as RESTATEMENT (a good answer to either question would largely answer the other, either direction: the D05 containment rule), CLOSE, INTERNAL_DUPLICATE or OK (92 OK, listed only by omission). The author (agent) rewrote the 4 RESTATEMENTs and 3 CLOSE pairs it judged restatements under the containment rule (wine glass vs violin bow, pine cones vs paper curling, termite mounds vs solar chimney), and reworded one question with a form problem (b2-the-natural-world-03). Each replacement was screened by keyword against both banks before use. Second pass: a fresh reviewer, blind to the first, checked the 8 replacements against both full lists (second_pass).

verdict_meanings.RESTATEMENT: keeps the overlap report unclean while the question is in the bank
verdict_meanings.OK: no historical or bank question asks this

findings.question: Why does an empty room echo more than the same room furnished?
findings.matched: How does a room change the sound of a live performance?
findings.rationale: A good answer on how a room shapes sound centres on hard surfaces reflecting and soft furnishings absorbing, which is the whole answer to the empty-versus-furnished echo question.

findings.question: How does a plastic bottle crumple as the hot air inside cools?
findings.matched: Why does a balloon shrink when you put it in the freezer?
findings.rationale: Both are answered by cooling gas losing pressure and volume so outside air pressure squeezes the container; same mechanism, different container.

findings.question: How does a flute sound a note when air is blown across a hole?
findings.matched: Explain how a whistle produces a steady tone.
findings.rationale: Both rest on the same edge-tone mechanism, an air jet split on a sharp edge driving a resonating air column, so one answer largely covers the other.

findings.question: How does a screen printer lay each colour of a design separately?
findings.matched: Explain how a printing press registers colours in sequence.
findings.rationale: Both are about printing one colour per pass from separate plates or screens and aligning them with registration; the screen-specific stencil detail is the only addition.

findings.question: Why do mapmakers shade hills as though lit from the upper left?
findings.matched: Describe why maps use contour lines.
findings.rationale: Both concern showing relief on a flat map, but hill shading explains a lighting convention and how people perceive it, while contours are about measured elevation.

findings.question: Why do enamel artists fire powdered glass onto copper several times?
findings.matched: How does a ceramic glaze change in the heat of a kiln?
findings.rationale: Both involve glassy coatings fused by firing, but the enamel question is about building layers through repeated firings on metal.

findings.question: How does a hat maker press felt into a firm lasting shape?
findings.matched: How does a shoemaker shape leather around a wooden last?
findings.rationale: Both are about moistening or heating a material and setting it over a wooden form, though felt and leather are stiffened differently.

findings.question: Why does chalk squeak on a blackboard when held at some angles?
findings.matched: Why do bicycle brakes sometimes squeal in wet weather?
findings.rationale: Both squeals come from stick-slip vibration, but the brake question turns on wet conditions and the chalk one on holding angle.

findings.question: Why does a wet finger make a wine glass sing around its rim?
findings.matched: Explain how a violin bow makes a string sound.
findings.rationale: Both use stick-slip friction to excite a resonator, but the wine glass answer centres on the glass bowl's own resonance.

findings.question: Why do cotton towels soak up water better than nylon ones?
findings.matched: Explain how a sponge holds and releases water.
findings.rationale: Both involve capillary uptake of water, but the towel question turns on hydrophilic cotton fibres versus water-repelling nylon.

findings.question: Why does boiling water poured into a cold glass sometimes crack it?
findings.matched: Describe why laboratory glassware is annealed.
findings.rationale: Both are about stress in glass, but thermal shock from uneven expansion differs from removing leftover manufacturing stress.

findings.question: How do glow in the dark stickers keep shining after lights go off?
findings.matched: What happens inside a glow stick when you snap it and it lights up?
findings.rationale: Both are about things that glow in the dark, but stickers store light (phosphorescence) while glow sticks light up by a chemical reaction (chemiluminescence).

findings.question: Why does mayonnaise thicken as oil is whisked in drop by drop?
findings.matched: How does the order of adding ingredients change a sauce?
findings.rationale: The order-of-ingredients answer could touch on adding oil slowly to an emulsion, but the mayonnaise answer centres on how the emulsion forms and is held stable.

findings.question: Why do cooks salt aubergine slices before frying them?
findings.matched: How does salt change the texture of vegetables as they cook?
findings.rationale: Both involve salt drawing water out by osmosis, but salting aubergine is a step before frying aimed at bitterness and oil uptake.

findings.question: Why does the first pancake from a pan so often turn out badly?
findings.matched: How does resting a batter improve pancakes?
findings.rationale: Both are about pancakes, but the first-pancake answer is about pan heat and oil, not the batter.

findings.question: How does a cook clarify butter to stop it burning?
findings.matched: What happens when butter is browned, and why do bakers treasure the result?
findings.rationale: Both turn on butter's milk solids browning under heat, one removing them to prevent burning and the other prizing the browned result.

findings.question: How do cooks poach an egg so that it holds its shape?
findings.matched: Why do eggs turn solid when they are cooked?
findings.rationale: Both involve egg proteins setting, but poaching technique (fresh eggs, gentle simmer, vinegar, swirl) is the core of the new answer.

findings.question: How does choux pastry puff up hollow inside the oven?
findings.matched: How does a souffle rise in the oven and why does it fall?
findings.rationale: Both are about puffing in the oven, but choux rises on steam and sets hollow, while a souffle rises on whipped egg foam and falls.

findings.question: How does a roux of flour and butter thicken a sauce?
findings.matched: How do blended vegetables thicken a soup without flour?
findings.rationale: Both are about thickening a liquid, but a roux works by starch gelatinising in fat-coated flour.

findings.question: How does a tandoor oven bake flatbread stuck to its walls?
findings.matched: How does a pizza stone help the crust cook evenly?
findings.rationale: Both bake bread on hot stored-heat masonry, but the tandoor answer covers dough sticking to a vertical wall and very high radiant heat.

findings.question: How do makers turn soya milk into firm blocks of tofu?
findings.matched: How does one basic ingredient, milk, become cheeses with such different textures and flavors?
findings.rationale: Both curdle milk proteins with a coagulant, but tofu is a single plant-protein coagulation, not cheese ripening.

findings.question: Why do the seasons fall at opposite times in the two hemispheres?
findings.matched: Why do polar regions swing between months of darkness and midnight sun?
findings.rationale: Both are explained by the tilt of the Earth's axis as it orbits, but the phenomena explained differ (opposite seasons versus polar day and night).

findings.question: Why does the date change for travellers crossing the middle of the Pacific?
findings.matched: Why do time zone boundaries zigzag around countries instead of following clean lines?
findings.rationale: Both concern time-keeping boundaries, but the date-line answer is about where the calendar day rolls over, not political zigzags.

findings.question: Why do some lone peaks trail a plume of cloud from one side?
findings.matched: How does a mountain range change the weather on either side?
findings.rationale: Both involve air forced over mountains, but banner clouds are a specific lee-side updraft effect around one isolated peak.

findings.question: Why does the soil look deep red across many tropical regions?
findings.matched: Why do lush rainforests often grow on surprisingly poor soils?
findings.rationale: Both arise from intense tropical weathering and leaching, but the new answer centres on iron oxides giving the red colour.

findings.question: How does a tidal bore send a wave racing up a river?
findings.matched: Why do tidal ranges vary so dramatically from one shore to another?
findings.rationale: A large tidal range in a funnel-shaped estuary is a precondition for a bore, but the bore's wave-front mechanism is a separate answer.

findings.question: How do terraced fields hold water on steep hillsides?
findings.matched: How does the slope of farmland affect the way it is worked?
findings.rationale: An answer about farming slopes would mention terracing, but the new question asks specifically how terraces hold water (level steps, retaining walls, bunds).

findings.question: Why does the stomach not digest its own lining?
findings.matched: How does the gut break food down into parts the body can use?
findings.rationale: Both concern digestion, but the new answer is about the mucus and bicarbonate barrier and cell renewal that protect the stomach lining.

findings.question: How do hands build calluses where they grip tools often?
findings.matched: How does the body respond to repeated small injuries?
findings.rationale: Calluses are one example of adapting to repeated friction, but the broad question goes beyond skin thickening.

findings.question: How do the vocal cords change pitch when a person sings higher?
findings.matched: Why does the voice deepen during the teenage years?
findings.rationale: Both rely on vocal fold length, tension and mass setting pitch, but one is growth during puberty and the other is muscle control while singing.

findings.question: How does steady practice make a physical skill feel automatic?
findings.matched: Why do musicians practise slowly to play quickly?
findings.rationale: Both concern motor learning, but the new question is about automaticity in general rather than the slow-practice strategy.

findings.question: Why did early photographs require sitters to hold still for so long?
findings.matched: Explain how a camera aperture controls exposure.
findings.rationale: Both involve exposure, but long sitting times came from insensitive early plates and processes, not aperture control.

findings.question: Why did the ancient Greeks build theatres into hillsides?
findings.matched: How does the shape of a concert hall affect what the audience hears?
findings.rationale: Hillside theatres partly concern acoustics, but the answer also covers sightlines, seating and saved building work.

findings.question: How did friction matches change the way people lit fires at home?
findings.matched: Why does a match need a rough surface to light?
findings.rationale: Same object, but the new question is about the social and household history rather than the chemistry of striking.

findings.question: How did ancient Egyptians make papyrus sheets from river reeds?
findings.matched: Explain how paper is made from wood pulp.
findings.rationale: Both are about making writing sheets from plant fibre, but papyrus is made from laminated strips of pith, not pulp.

findings.question: Why do recipes give each of their steps as a direct command?
findings.matched: What makes a set of instructions genuinely easy to follow?
findings.rationale: Both concern instructional writing, but the new question targets the imperative mood convention specifically.

findings.question: How does a limerick build its bouncing rhythm across five lines?
findings.matched: How does rhythm affect whether a line of poetry stays in memory?
findings.rationale: Both concern poetic rhythm, but the limerick question is about how its specific metre and rhyme scheme are built.

findings.question: How does a spoonerism swap sounds to make a comic phrase?
findings.matched: How does a tongue twister trip up the person saying it?
findings.rationale: Both involve swapped or confused speech sounds, but spoonerisms are about deliberate sound transposition used for comedy.

findings.question: How does an electric guitar pickup sense the movement of steel strings?
findings.matched: Explain how a microphone turns sound into a signal.
findings.rationale: Both turn movement into an electrical signal, often by magnetic induction, but a pickup senses steel strings disturbing a magnet's field, not air pressure.

findings.question: How are steel pans hammered so that one drum plays many notes?
findings.matched: How does a xylophone get different pitches from bars of wood?
findings.rationale: Both are about getting several pitches from one percussion instrument, but steel pans rely on hammered, tuned areas of a single sheet of metal.

findings.question: Why are javelins made to land point first?
findings.matched: How does a shuttlecock always turn to fly cork first?
findings.rationale: Both rest on the centre of mass sitting ahead of the centre of pressure, but the javelin question also covers the rule change and the reasons for measuring.

findings.question: Why does topspin make a table tennis ball dip onto the table?
findings.matched: Why does a curved run-up help a footballer bend a free kick?
findings.rationale: Both involve the Magnus effect on a spinning ball, but the new answer concerns topspin making the ball dip and kick off the table.

findings.question: Why do induction hobs heat a pan while the glass stays fairly cool?
findings.matched: How do microwave ovens heat the food without strongly heating the plate beneath it?
findings.rationale: The same 'heats food, not the dish' puzzle, but induction works by eddy currents in a ferrous pan rather than microwaves exciting water.

findings.question: How does a phone know to turn its screen when held sideways?
findings.matched: How does a smartwatch approximate the steps someone takes?
findings.rationale: Both rely on accelerometers, but screen rotation reads the direction of gravity rather than counting motion patterns.

findings.question: How does a speed camera measure the speed of a passing car?
findings.matched: Why does the pitch of a passing siren seem to change?
findings.rationale: Radar speed cameras use the Doppler shift, but the answer also covers radar, laser timing and camera triggering.

findings.question: Why do dogs pant to cool down rather than sweat?
findings.matched: How does the body regulate its temperature on a very hot day?
findings.rationale: Both are about shedding heat by evaporation, but panting uses the airways and suits a dog's fur and few sweat glands.
findings.form_problem: Minor premise simplification: dogs do sweat a little through their paw pads, so 'rather than sweat' is not strictly true.

findings.question: Why do cactus plants bear spines where other plants grow leaves?
findings.matched: Why do desert plants often have waxy surfaces and deep roots?
findings.rationale: Both concern cactus adaptations to dry places, but spines as reduced leaves (less water loss, defence, shade) are a different answer.

findings.question: How does a snail build its shell larger as it grows?
findings.matched: How do crabs grow when they are covered in a hard shell?
findings.rationale: Both ask how a shelled animal grows, but snails add to the shell edge while crabs moult.

findings.question: How do termites build mounds that stay cool inside?
findings.matched: Explain how a solar chimney drives ventilation.
findings.rationale: Termite mound cooling is often explained by chimney-style airflow, but the answer also covers porous walls and how the colony works.

findings.question: How do pine cones open and close with the weather?
findings.matched: Why does a sheet of paper curl when one side gets damp?
findings.rationale: Both are moisture-driven bending, where one layer swells more than the other, but pine cones open and close through two layers of differing tissue.

findings.question: How does a sorting office route letters using their postcodes?
findings.matched: How did street numbering change the delivery of letters?
findings.rationale: Both concern addressing systems for mail, but the new answer is about machine and manual sorting by postcode, not history.

findings.question: How does a newsroom choose which story leads the front page?
findings.matched: How does a journalist decide what belongs in the opening sentence?
findings.rationale: Both concern editorial prominence, but choosing a front-page lead is a newsroom decision across stories, not the lead sentence of one story.

findings.question: How does a hook and loop fastener grip and then peel apart?
findings.matched: Explain how a zip fastener holds two edges together.
findings.rationale: Different fastener with a different mechanism; only the broad fastener subject overlaps.

findings.rationale: No eraser or graphite question exists.

findings.question: Why do thin foil blankets help keep a cold runner warm?
findings.rationale: No survival or space blanket question; nearest are generic insulation or penguin items on different subjects.

findings.rationale: Both concern animal navigation, but this one is specific to salmon natal homing, so an answer would only partly cover the general question.

findings.question: How does a chameleon aim its tongue at a distant insect?
findings.rationale: No chameleon or projectile tongue question exists.
